trial_name: Hemodiafe — Continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration versus intermittent haemodialysis for acute renal failure in patients with multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (2006)
citation: Vinsonneau C, Camus C, Combes A, Costa de Beauregard MA, Klouche K, Boulain T, et al; Hemodiafe Study Group. Continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration versus intermittent haemodialysis for acute renal failure in patients with multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome: a multicentre randomised trial. Lancet. 2006;368:379-85.
one_liner: In ICU patients with acute renal failure and MODS, CVVHDF did not improve 60-day survival compared with IHD (32.6% vs 31.5%, absolute difference 1.1%, 95% CI -8.8 to 11.1, P=0.98).

pico.population: Critically ill adults with acute renal failure and MODS requiring RRT (LOD score ≥6, urea ≥36 mmol/L or creatinine ≥310 μmol/L; later oliguria <320 mL/16h added)
pico.intervention: Continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) with mean blood flow 145.7 mL/min, dialysate flow 1099 mL/h, ultrafiltration/replacement flow 1278 mL/h, average dose 29 mL/kg/h
pico.comparison: Intermittent haemodialysis (IHD) with daily sessions, mean duration 5.2 h, blood flow 278 mL/min, dialysate flow 500 mL/min, with haemodynamic-tolerance strategies (high sodium, cool dialysate)

background.existing_knowledge: Acute kidney injury requiring RRT in ICU patients with MODS carries high mortality. IHD and CRRT were both widely used, with physiological arguments and practice variation. Pre-trial evidence consisted of single-centre experience, small randomised studies, and confounded observational comparisons; it was unclear whether modality choice affected survival, renal recovery, or treatment tolerance.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether CVVHDF improves survival compared with IHD in severe ICU AKI with MODS.
background.hypothesis: CVVHDF would improve 60-day survival compared with IHD.

methods.design: Prospective, multicentre, parallel-group, open-label, randomised trial in 21 ICUs in France (Oct 1999–Mar 2003); allocation stratified by centre; outcome assessors blinded.
methods.setting: 21 medical or multidisciplinary ICUs in France.

inclusion: Need for RRT plus severe MODS (LOD score ≥6) and biochemical criteria (serum urea ≥36 mmol/L and/or serum creatinine ≥310 μmol/L); after ~8 months, oliguria (<320 mL over 16 h despite fluid loading) was added due to low enrolment.
exclusion: Age <18 years; pregnancy; pre-existing chronic renal failure (pre-ARF serum creatinine >180 μmol/L); obstructive or vascular aetiology of acute renal failure; ongoing ACE inhibitor exposure; major bleeding risk (prothrombin time <20% and/or platelets <30×10^9/L) or uncontrolled haemorrhage; SAPS II ≤37; moribund/expected survival <8 days.

methods.intervention: CVVHDF: Delivered with Aquarius system; mean blood flow 145.7 mL/min (95% CI 138.7–152.8); dialysate flow 1099 mL/h (1053–1145); ultrafiltration/replacement flow 1278 mL/h (1222–1334); average dose 29 mL/kg/h; net fluid removal 2107 mL/day (1738–2476); anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin when feasible, non-heparin strategies if contraindicated.
methods.comparison: IHD: Recommended daily sessions; mean session duration 5.2 h (95% CI 4.9–5.6); blood flow 278 mL/min (269–288); dialysate flow 500 mL/min (fixed); net ultrafiltration 2213 mL/day (1944–2482); haemodynamic-tolerance strategies: high sodium dialysate ~145 mmol/L and cool dialysate ~35°C during first 24 h. Switching to other modality permitted if clinically necessary.
methods.blinding: Non-blinded treatment allocation; outcome assessors reported as blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: Initially planned 480 patients (240/group) to detect 10% absolute increase in survival (50% to 60%) with 80% power at α=0.05; after early observed survival ~22%, recalculated to 360 patients (180/group) for same absolute difference; primary analysis intention-to-treat.
methods.follow_up: 60 days (primary), with additional day 28 and day 90 survival; renal recovery/dialysis dependence assessed in survivors after ICU and hospital discharge.

headline_bullets: Neutral primary endpoint: Day 60 survival essentially identical (CVVHDF 32.6% vs IHD 31.5%; absolute difference 1.1%; 95% CI -8.8 to 11.1; P=0.98).
System-level outcomes similar: Renal support duration (11 vs 11 days), ICU stay (19 vs 20 days), hospital stay (32 vs 30 days) did not differ (all P>0.6).
Safety/tolerability signal: Hypothermia more frequent with CVVHDF (17% vs 5%; P=0.0005), and unplanned switching more frequent from CVVHDF to IHD (10% vs 3%; P=0.01).

outcomes_table.note: Intention-to-treat; no evidence of survival benefit with CVVHDF.

outcomes_table.outcome: Dialysis dependence after ICU discharge (among assessed survivors)
Unplanned switch to the other modality
outcomes_table.note: Switching permitted; higher switching from CVVHDF to IHD.

safety: Hypothermia occurred more often with CVVHDF (17% vs 5%; P=0.0005).
Unplanned switching from CVVHDF to IHD was more frequent (10% vs 3%; P=0.01).

domains.notes: Central computer-generated randomisation, balanced blocks of four, stratified by centre; allocation concealed until enrolment complete.
Open-label delivery creates risk for clinician-mediated outcomes (switching, RRT discontinuation), though primary outcome (mortality) is objective; outcome assessors reported as blinded.
360 randomised (184 IHD, 176 CVVHDF); 1 patient in CVVHDF group withdrew consent and excluded from analysis; no other loss to follow-up for survival endpoints.

IHD delivered: mean session duration 5.2 h, blood flow 278 mL/min, dialysate flow 500 mL/min. CVVHDF delivered: blood flow 145.7 mL/min, dialysate flow 1099 mL/h, ultrafiltration/replacement flow 1278 mL/h, average dose 29 mL/kg/h. Biochemical separation in azotaemia small (mean urea 14.8 vs 15.7 mmol/L). Unplanned switching more frequent in CVVHDF arm (10% vs 3%), potentially diluting modality effect.
Groups well matched on key severity indicators (mean SAPS II ~64–65; mean LOD ~10; high prevalence of mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support).
Enrolment occurred early-to-intermediate in ICU course (median ~2–3 days after ICU admission), but not ultra-early; AKI pathobiology may already have been established.
Multicentre conduct increases generalisability, but centre-level practice differences and permitted switching introduce treatment heterogeneity; no major centre interaction highlighted.
Intention-to-treat analysis; sample size revision and lower-than-anticipated survival reduce precision; confidence interval around primary effect permits modest benefit or harm.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears moderate to strong for the mortality endpoint (robust randomisation; objective outcome; minimal attrition), but is limited for modality-specific mechanistic inference due to open-label care, substantial switching (especially from CVVHDF to IHD), and imperfect comparability of delivered 'dose' metrics across modalities.

domains.notes: Highly representative of severe ICU AKI with MODS (very high rates of mechanical ventilation and vasopressor use; majority septic), but not representative of milder AKI (SAPS II ≤37 excluded) or patients with significant pre-existing chronic kidney disease.

Both modalities delivered with relatively optimised prescriptions (e.g., haemodynamic-tolerance strategies for IHD; quantified CVVHDF dose), which may exceed consistency achievable in less-resourced settings. Findings most applicable to centres that can deliver both IHD and CVVHDF at high quality with experienced staff; comparative balance may differ where one modality is delivered suboptimally or staffing constraints limit continuous therapies.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is good to high-acuity ICUs managing severe AKI with MODS in well-resourced settings, but more limited for less severe AKI, pre-existing advanced CKD, and settings where consistent delivery of either modality (particularly CVVHDF) is constrained.

strengths: Pragmatic allowance of switching reflecting real-world practice
Detailed reporting of delivered treatment parameters and adverse events
limitations: Substantial switching/crossover (especially from CVVHDF to IHD) potentially diluting modality effects
'Dose' comparability between IHD and CVVHDF remains methodologically challenging
Inclusion criteria amended early in the trial (oliguria added) with potential for population drift

critical_appraisal.summary: Hemodiafe is a well-conducted multicentre RCT with robust randomisation and objective primary outcome, but open-label design, substantial crossover, and imperfect dose comparability limit confidence in modality-specific mechanistic inferences; the neutral result for survival is credible, but the trial does not exclude modest benefit or harm.
strengths: High-risk population with high event rate
weaknesses: Dose comparability between modalities not directly equivalent

sections.authors_conclusion: When both modalities are delivered with careful prescriptions, CVVHDF did not improve survival over IHD in severe ICU AKI with MODS; modality choice should therefore prioritise haemodynamic stability, fluid balance needs, anticoagulation constraints, staffing, and local expertise.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: CVVHDF does not improve survival over IHD in severe ICU AKI with MODS; modality choice should be individualised based on haemodynamics, fluid goals, anticoagulation feasibility, and local capability rather than expecting a mortality benefit from continuous therapy alone.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Severe ICU AKI with MODS in well-resourced settings where both modalities can be delivered optimally.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That continuous modalities are inferior or should be abandoned; they may still be preferred for haemodynamic instability or fluid management, but not for survival benefit.
implementation_caveats: Ensure high-quality delivery of whichever modality is chosen (dose, continuity, complication prevention).
Monitor for and prevent hypothermia during CVVHDF.
Permit rational switching between modalities based on clinical need rather than rigid protocol adherence.

controversies.notes: The accompanying editorial argued that, in a setting where both treatments are delivered competently, the absence of a mortality difference supports prioritising high-quality delivery (dose, continuity, complication prevention) over claims of intrinsic modality superiority.

controversies.topic: Switching as both strength and threat
controversies.notes: Permitting switching improves pragmatic relevance, but higher switching from CVVHDF to IHD (10% vs 3%) can dilute effect estimates and makes 'pure modality' comparisons harder to interpret as causal.

Systematic reviews aggregating randomised evidence have not demonstrated a consistent mortality advantage for continuous over intermittent modalities; differences, where present, tend to relate to haemodynamic tolerance and selected renal-recovery outcomes rather than survival.

KDIGO recommends individualising modality choice, commonly favouring continuous modalities in haemodynamically unstable patients, while acknowledging the low-to-moderate certainty of evidence for hard outcomes. Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines similarly do not endorse a universal survival benefit of one RRT modality and emphasise choosing a strategy consistent with haemodynamics, fluid management goals, and available resources.

unresolved_questions: Does CVVHDF improve renal recovery or long-term dialysis dependence compared with IHD?
What is the optimal delivered dose for IHD to achieve comparable solute control to CVVHDF?
How does modality choice affect long-term patient-centred outcomes (quality of life, functional status)?

numbers_to_remember: 60-day survival: CVVHDF 32.6% vs IHD 31.5% (absolute difference 1.1%, 95% CI -8.8 to 11.1, P=0.98)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In severe ICU AKI with MODS, CVVHDF does not improve survival over optimised IHD; choose modality based on haemodynamics, fluid goals, and local capability, not expected mortality benefit.
